customs.name: Domestic holy-water font / bénitier de chevet
customs.canonical_statement: A bedside or domestic bénitier holding blessed water is a documented French Catholic domestic object and devotional custom.
customs.period_label: 19th–20th c.; pre-conciliar
customs.guardrail: Present as a historical/traditional domestic practice, not a requirement.

customs.name: Family consecration to the Sacred Heart
customs.canonical_statement: Family consecration to the Sacred Heart is a well-attested French devotional practice centered on Paray-le-Monial and may be presented as a voluntary devotion.
customs.period_label: 19th c. → present
customs.calendar_trigger_hint: Sacred Heart season / family use
customs.guardrail: Keep distinct from the liturgy and from priestly house blessing.

customs.name: Intronement of a Sacred Heart image in the home
customs.canonical_statement: The enthronement/intronisation of the Sacred Heart image is a documented French family devotion. It is not universal liturgical law.
customs.period_label: Late 19th–20th c. → present
customs.guardrail: Any blessing of the image remains ministerial where required.

customs.name: Relevailles / blessing after childbirth
customs.canonical_statement: Relevailles are a voluntary thanksgiving/blessing after childbirth. They are not a purification from ritual impurity and no mandatory forty-day waiting period should be taught.
customs.period_label: Pre-conciliar; historical today
customs.guardrail: Preserve the anti-misconception note prominently.

customs.name: May as the month of Mary
customs.canonical_statement: The month of May has a long-standing Catholic Marian devotional association and strong French-world attestation. It is devotional custom, not part of the formal liturgical calendar structure.
customs.period_label: Early modern → present
customs.calendar_trigger_hint: May
customs.guardrail: Calendar points to the practice; devotional modules own prayer content.

customs.name: Pilgrimage to a shrine or holy place
customs.canonical_statement: Pilgrimage is a legitimate personal or collective act of Catholic piety. It is commendable and optional, not a universal obligation.
customs.period_label: Ancient → present
customs.guardrail: Do not turn local pilgrimage calendars into universal app law.

customs.name: Regional pardons and shrine anniversaries
customs.canonical_statement: Regional pilgrimages and pardons are genuine Catholic customs but belong to local metadata, not the universal Ad Orientem calendar.
customs.period_label: Varies
customs.decision: KEEP — EXAMPLE ONLY / NO GLOBAL ENGINE
customs.guardrail: No country mode and no universal trigger.

customs.name: Ex-votos
customs.canonical_statement: Ex-votos are documented French Catholic offerings of thanksgiving/testimony at shrines. They should be explained as expressions of gratitude, not magical transactions.
customs.period_label: 17th c. → present
customs.guardrail: Avoid superstition framing.

customs.name: Votive candle at a shrine
customs.canonical_statement: Lighting a votive candle at a shrine is a documented devotional act; the flame symbolizes and prolongs prayer rather than functioning magically.
customs.period_label: Longstanding → present
customs.guardrail: Do not imply payment purchases spiritual effects.

customs.name: Prayerful cemetery visit
customs.canonical_statement: Visiting a cemetery to pray for the dead is an established Catholic devotional practice and strongly French-attested.
customs.period_label: Longstanding → present
customs.calendar_trigger_hint: 02/11; November; anniversaries
customs.guardrail: Explain as prayer and bonds with the dead, not superstitious obligation.

customs.name: Prayer for the dead on 2 November
customs.canonical_statement: 2 November is a privileged day of prayer for the faithful departed; cemetery visits are common but the core is prayer for the dead.
customs.period_label: Liturgical observance → present
customs.guardrail: Calendar owns the date; Pray owns prayer texts.

customs.name: Glas / death bell
customs.canonical_statement: The glas is a French Catholic bell custom announcing death or obsequies. The generic meaning is suitable for formation; exact strike patterns are highly local.
customs.period_label: Historical → present in places
customs.guardrail: Do not encode local sex/age/number-of-strokes patterns as universal.

customs.name: Pain bénit
customs.canonical_statement: Pain bénit is a historical French Catholic parish custom: blessed bread distinct from the Eucharist. It is local/regional and should not be implied as a universal Roman practice.
customs.period_label: Historical; largely declined
customs.guardrail: Distinguish clearly from the Eucharist; stronger historical source closure is still desirable.

customs.name: Using holy water at home
customs.canonical_statement: Keeping and using genuinely blessed holy water in the home is a traditional Catholic sacramental practice. French domestic bénitiers attest the custom; the blessing of the water itself is distinct from a layperson’s personal devotional use.
customs.period_label: Pre-conciliar → present
customs.guardrail: Using holy water is voluntary and is not a substitute for sacramental worship; do not reproduce or claim to perform reserved blessings. Keep distinct from DOM-002, which documents the vessel.

customs.name: Keeping blessed Candlemas candles at home
customs.canonical_statement: Catholic families have traditionally taken blessed candles home after the Candlemas liturgy. Their light recalls Christ, light for the nations; their devotional use is neither compulsory nor a guarantee of physical protection.
customs.period_label: Historical domestic practice → present
customs.calendar_trigger_hint: 02/02 — Candlemas (date owned by Calendar)
customs.guardrail: The 1962 Candlemas reader owns the liturgical blessing and procession; no home ritual is mandated. Historical use near the dying is contextual, never an obligation.

customs.name: Keeping blessed Palm Sunday branches at home
customs.canonical_statement: The faithful traditionally take blessed Palm Sunday branches home, including to adorn domestic crucifixes as a sign of trust in Christ crucified. This follows, rather than replaces, participation in the Palm Sunday liturgy.
customs.period_label: Historical practice → present
customs.calendar_trigger_hint: Palm Sunday (calculated by Calendar)
customs.guardrail: Blessed branches are not talismans; branches and regional plant species vary. The Palm Sunday reader retains exclusive ownership of ceremonial mechanics.

customs.name: St Blaise — blessing of throats
customs.canonical_statement: On or near 3 February, Catholics may receive a traditional blessing invoking St Blaise's intercession against ailments of the throat and other illnesses. In the historical Roman Ritual a priest blesses candles specifically for this blessing and applies two crossed candles while praying; the modern Book of Blessings provides different candle and ministerial provisions.
customs.period_label: Pre-1962 Roman Ritual witness → current practice in distinct ritual forms
customs.calendar_trigger_hint: 03/02, St Blaise commemoration in 1962 Roman calendar; Calendar owns calculation and precedence
customs.guardrail: Voluntary, not a Mass or a third-class feast in the ordinary 1962 calendar, not a promise of healing, and no app-provided or lay-invented priestly ceremony. The historical St Blaise candle blessing and modern Candlemas-candle provision must not be equated. Availability varies by parish.

customs.name: Baptismal patron's name day
customs.canonical_statement: Families may commemorate a person's baptismal patron on that saint's feast with prayer, the saint's life and a modest family meal, optionally attending Mass; this is a voluntary domestic celebration, not an additional liturgical feast.
customs.period_label: Traditional Catholic family practice; 1962 Catholic household witness
customs.guardrail: Only display after a user chooses a patron and the relevant traditional saint feast. Never infer a patron from a first name, invent an obligation, or create a second feast.

customs.name: French fête patronale / village patronal celebration
customs.canonical_statement: A French local church or village may observe its own patronal feast with Mass, procession and communal festivities; the particular date and form belong to the local place and are not universally scheduled.
customs.period_label: Medieval roots; locally continuing example at Chantelle
customs.guardrail: The documented Chantelle celebration after Ascension does not establish a national date, a 1962 Mass rank or automatic procession.

customs.name: French Assumption Marian processions
customs.canonical_statement: In documented French localities the Assumption is celebrated with public Marian processions, sometimes carrying a statue of Our Lady. Participation is voluntary and dependent on an actual locally announced event.
customs.period_label: Historical → documented 2026
customs.calendar_trigger_hint: 15/08 — Assumption; regional context, never automatic ritual
customs.guardrail: The feast date is not a procession flag. Existing Mass and ceremonial reader remains exclusively responsible for an explicitly selected local rite.

customs.name: St Joseph's table and gifts to the poor
customs.canonical_statement: The Sicilian-rooted St Joseph table is a charitable feast custom involving a display or sharing of food and support for people in need, with documented modern parish celebrations around 19 March.
customs.period_label: Sicilian tradition → 2026 US diocesan celebration
customs.calendar_trigger_hint: 19/03 — St Joseph feast; optional local family and parish practice
customs.guardrail: A domestic St Joseph table is not the celebration of a Mass or a lay-performed priestly blessing. Do not present specific pastries, miracle accounts or dates of transferred Masses as established.

customs.name: St Anthony's Bread / Pain des pauvres
customs.canonical_statement: The Franciscan charitable practice of St Anthony's Bread supports people in need; its French revival is associated with Louise Bouffier of Toulon in 1890. Families may honour the saint with voluntary almsgiving.
customs.period_label: Late nineteenth century France → continuing Franciscan charitable witness
customs.calendar_trigger_hint: 13/06 — St Anthony of Padua; charity can be practised on any day
customs.guardrail: Almsgiving is not a payment for favours, fundraising functionality, or a guarantee of a miracle. No contact or money spending is required by the app.

customs.name: St Christopher — vehicles and travellers' blessing
customs.canonical_statement: Some French parishes celebrate St Christopher and arrange a ministerial blessing of drivers, travellers and vehicles near 25 July; one 2026 parish example took place on 19 July.
customs.period_label: Historical tradition → 2026 parish witness
customs.calendar_trigger_hint: 25/07 — St Christopher commemoration; parish event date may differ
customs.guardrail: Optional and only if arranged locally; no guarantee of physical safety, no invented lay blessing formula, no universal parish offering.

customs.name: St Nicholas's visit and small gifts to children
customs.canonical_statement: In parts of Alsace and Lorraine, families and communities mark St Nicholas's 6 December feast with a costumed visitor, treats or modest gifts, and stories that can lead children toward the saint's Christian charity.
customs.period_label: Regional tradition → documented contemporary Alsatian practice
customs.calendar_trigger_hint: 06/12 — St Nicholas; regional household custom
customs.guardrail: The historical biography of Nicholas must be distinguished from later folklore. Exclude threatening costumed helpers and claims that gifts are liturgically required.

customs.name: Assumption — blessing of herbs, flowers and fruits
customs.canonical_statement: In parts of Catholic Europe, especially historically Germanic regions, herbs, flowers and the fruits of the earth are brought for a priestly blessing on the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary (15 August). The Roman Ritual includes an appropriate traditional blessing, while local provision varies.
customs.period_label: Medieval regional practice; received into historical Roman Ritual; observed in some places today
customs.calendar_trigger_hint: 15 August, Assumption; date and Mass rank owned by Calendar
customs.guardrail: Do not present as mandatory, universal, a guarantee of healing, or a magical protection. No Mass/ceremonial mechanics or ministerial blessing formula in lay guidance. Availability depends on local clergy.

customs.name: St John the Evangelist — blessing of wine
customs.canonical_statement: A documented traditional Catholic custom on 27 December is to bring wine to be blessed by a priest in honour of St John the Evangelist. This custom is preserved in historical Roman Ritual material and local Catholic practice; the associated account of poisoned wine is traditional legend, not a proven historical episode.
customs.period_label: Historic Central European and Roman-rite devotional custom; locally continued
customs.calendar_trigger_hint: 27 December, feast of St John the Apostle and Evangelist in 1962 Roman calendar
customs.guardrail: No implication that wine is the Precious Blood, automatic protection, universal parish availability, medical treatment, compulsory drinking or an invitation to drink alcohol. Blessing is ministerial.

customs.name: Holy Saturday — blessing of Easter foods
customs.canonical_statement: In several Catholic regional traditions, especially Polish and other Central/Eastern European households, families bring eggs, bread and other Easter foods to be blessed by an authorised minister, often on Holy Saturday. The foods are subsequently shared at Easter; the historical Roman Ritual includes blessings of lamb, eggs and bread.
customs.period_label: Pre-conciliar → present, regionally variable
customs.calendar_trigger_hint: Holy Saturday (calculated from 1962 Easter by Calendar), with domestic use on Easter Sunday
customs.guardrail: No obligation, no universal standard basket contents or Holy Saturday schedule. Distinguish a minister's ritual blessing from family prayer before the Easter meal and do not displace the Easter Vigil.

customs.name: Family Advent wreath and Sunday candle prayer
customs.canonical_statement: The family Advent wreath, commonly made with four candles, accompanies prayer and Scripture during Advent; additional candles are traditionally lit on successive Sundays as the Nativity approaches.
customs.period_label: Catholic family Advent practice, contemporary episcopal witness
customs.decision: KEEP — SOURCE-LOCKED WEISER P0 SIX PR
customs.calendar_trigger_hint: First Sunday of Advent; date owned by Calendar, no feast added
customs.guardrail: Household devotion only, not an ancient universal Roman rubric. Church and home blessing texts differ across rites and periods; do not insert modern blessing text or priestly gestures into the 1962 Mass.

customs.name: Advent manger straw after acts of charity
customs.canonical_statement: In a traditional Advent household activity, family members place straw in an empty manger after an act of kindness or prayer, preparing symbolically for the placement of the Christ Child at Christmas.
customs.period_label: Traditional attribution to French custom; independently documented in a Catholic US family in 2014
customs.decision: KEEP — SOURCE-LOCKED WEISER P0 SIX PR
customs.calendar_trigger_hint: Advent household preparation; Calendar owns liturgical dates
customs.guardrail: The French origin is a reported attribution, not certification of universal French practice. No in-app good-deed scoring, merit counting, sacramental or required custom.

customs.name: Las Posadas — Holy Family lodging procession
customs.canonical_statement: In Las Posadas, neighbours and families recall Mary and Joseph's search for lodging through songs and symbolic visits between houses, traditionally beginning on 16 December in Mexico and other Latin American Catholic communities.
customs.period_label: Traditional Catholic Mexican and wider Latin American Advent practice; USCCB modern confirmation
customs.decision: KEEP — SOURCE-LOCKED WEISER P0 SIX PR
customs.calendar_trigger_hint: 16–24 December in communities that actually celebrate Posadas
customs.guardrail: Regional and optional, not a ninth-day 1962 Mass formulary, compulsory celebration, default parish procession, confirmed public route or permission for a priestly ritual.

customs.name: Sharing opłatek on Polish Christmas Eve
customs.canonical_statement: Polish Catholic families may share thin unconsecrated opłatek wafers before Christmas Eve supper, exchanging wishes for peace and reconciliation. An optional blessing of the wafers by a priest is separate from the family sharing.
customs.period_label: Polish Catholic heritage observed in families and a US parish
customs.decision: KEEP — SOURCE-LOCKED WEISER P0 SIX PR
customs.calendar_trigger_hint: 24 December as customary domestic vigil, distinct from Mass
customs.guardrail: Opłatek is not the Eucharist or consecrated host; no pretend Communion, required priestly home blessing, universal Christmas obligation or fabricated fixed 1962 liturgical formula.

customs.name: Holy Thursday visits to altars of repose
customs.canonical_statement: Some Catholics visit several churches after the Holy Thursday Mass to pray before the Blessed Sacrament reserved at the altar of repose; seven stops is a customary number, not a requirement.
customs.period_label: Longstanding Catholic lay pilgrimage custom; 2026 diocesan press witness
customs.decision: KEEP — SOURCE-LOCKED WEISER P0 SIX PR
customs.calendar_trigger_hint: Holy Thursday, calculated from Easter by Calendar; locally open repositories only
customs.guardrail: Visits only to actually accessible churches; no inferred schedule, map route, obligatory seven stops, priestly ceremony or new event in the Mass reader.

customs.name: Family Rogation walk and prayer for the harvest
customs.canonical_statement: A family may mark the Rogation days with a private prayerful walk, asking God to bless the work of farmers and the fruits of the earth, distinct from any priest-led Rogation procession or ministerial blessing.
customs.period_label: 1956 independently documented Catholic family handbook practice
customs.decision: KEEP — SOURCE-LOCKED WEISER P0 SIX PR
customs.calendar_trigger_hint: Major Rogation 25 April and the three Minor Rogation days before Ascension; Calendar owns calculation
customs.guardrail: Domestic walk is voluntary and never an automatic liturgical procession; omit historical family's improvised blessings or ceremonial imitation. No rite, invented route, farm proximity requirement or 1962 rubric change.

customs.name: German Epiphany star singers / Sternsinger
customs.canonical_statement: Catholic children dressed as the Magi visit homes around Epiphany with song, blessings conveyed in the custom and charitable collections for children in need.
customs.period_label: Historical traditional practice with bounded contemporary or institutional witness
customs.decision: KEEP — SOURCE-LOCKED WEISER P1 FIVE DRAFT
customs.calendar_trigger_hint: 6 January, as a regional practice; visits must be locally announced
customs.guardrail: This is a German organised Catholic charitable custom, not universal priestly house blessing. Never infer local schedules, rites, donations or 1962 ceremony.

customs.name: French Galette des Rois and the poor person's portion
customs.canonical_statement: French Catholic households share a galette or King Cake with a fève; some traditional forms reserve an extra portion for someone poor or a guest.
customs.period_label: Historical traditional practice with bounded contemporary or institutional witness
customs.decision: KEEP — SOURCE-LOCKED WEISER P1 FIVE DRAFT
customs.calendar_trigger_hint: 6 January in the 1962 calendar; household celebration date may differ
customs.guardrail: Optional French household culture; the separate Weiser school-fees claim is not independently corroborated and is excluded.

customs.name: Corpus Christi flower carpets and window decorations
customs.canonical_statement: Some Catholic communities arrange flower carpets along Corpus Christi processional routes; in others flowers adorn streets and windows as expressions of reverence for the Blessed Sacrament.
customs.period_label: Historical traditional practice with bounded contemporary or institutional witness
customs.decision: KEEP — SOURCE-LOCKED WEISER P1 FIVE DRAFT
customs.calendar_trigger_hint: Corpus Christi where a real procession is celebrated locally
customs.guardrail: One canonical ID for two distinct regional floral forms. Neither a procession route nor a priestly blessing is automatically created. Weiser's precise candles-and-images claim is unverified.

customs.name: Easter Monday Emmaus walk
customs.canonical_statement: Catholics in parts of southern Germany and Austria take a family or parish walk on Easter Monday recalling the disciples who encountered the risen Christ on the road to Emmaus (Luke 24:13–35).
customs.period_label: Historical traditional practice with bounded contemporary or institutional witness
customs.decision: KEEP — SOURCE-LOCKED WEISER P1 FIVE DRAFT
customs.calendar_trigger_hint: Easter Monday calculated by Calendar; regional voluntary practice
customs.guardrail: No invented itinerary, time, local event or Eucharistic procession. Optional regional custom, separate from the 1962 Mass.

customs.name: Mary garden — flowers and herbs dedicated to Our Lady
customs.canonical_statement: A Catholic home may keep a small Mary garden or planters with flowers and herbs that recall Our Lady and invite prayer; individual plant legends require historical verification.
customs.period_label: Historical traditional practice with bounded contemporary or institutional witness
customs.decision: KEEP — SOURCE-LOCKED WEISER P1 FIVE DRAFT
customs.calendar_trigger_hint: May or another suitable gardening season; linked to DEV-001
customs.guardrail: Voluntary household devotion connected to existing May custom DEV-001, not a new feast. No magical, medicinal or historically unsupported plant properties.

customs.name: Epiphany doorway chalking (C+M+B)
customs.canonical_statement: Some Catholic families mark the doorway at Epiphany with the Cross, the year and the letters C+M+B, praying that Christ bless their home. The family gesture is optional and distinct from the priest's blessing of a house.
customs.period_label: Historically attested Epiphany devotion; modern episcopal pastoral witness
customs.calendar_trigger_hint: 6 January (Epiphany); preparations may begin shortly beforehand; no universal parish blessing schedule
customs.guardrail: Family chalking is not the priest's Roman Ritual blessing. Chalk may already have been blessed; do not imply this marking guarantees protection, makes a new rubric, or authorizes lay imitation of priest-only formulas.

customs.name: Keeping the Nativity crib until Candlemas
customs.canonical_statement: Some Catholic families keep their Nativity crib until Candlemas on 2 February and put it away after the feast. This is a voluntary household custom; it does not determine when Christmastide ends in the 1962 liturgical calendar.
customs.period_label: Historical European household usage; modern Catholic commentary records variable practice
customs.calendar_trigger_hint: 2 February household context; distinct from Candlemas candle blessing and liturgical season
customs.guardrail: Neither compulsory parish decoration rule nor Mass rite. Candlemas does not extend the 1962 Christmas liturgical season; this custom is not a continuation of the DOM-011 blessed candle practice.

attestations.period_label: Late nineteenth century France → continuing Franciscan charitable witness
attestations.evidence_note: WEI58-27-023. The Franciscan charitable practice of St Anthony's Bread supports people in need; its French revival is associated with Louise Bouffier of Toulon in 1890. Families may honour the saint with voluntary almsgiving.
WEI58-28-011. Some French parishes celebrate St Christopher and arrange a ministerial blessing of drivers, travellers and vehicles near 25 July; one 2026 parish example took place on 19 July.

attestations.period_label: Regional tradition → documented contemporary Alsatian practice
attestations.evidence_note: WEI58-28-020. In parts of Alsace and Lorraine, families and communities mark St Nicholas's 6 December feast with a costumed visitor, treats or modest gifts, and stories that can lead children toward the saint's Christian charity.
Wypominki remembrance lists name the deceased for parish prayer and memorial intentions; this enriches DEAD-003 and does not create a second universal Souls feast.

attestations.period_label: Historical Roman Ritual includes feast-specific blessing; regionally practised
attestations.evidence_note: The Roman rite has a traditional herb/fruit blessing for 15 August, specifically associated by the Vatican Directory with Germanic countries; a traditional Massachusetts parish independently documents local practice. World context describes the rite, not universal performance.

attestations.period_label: Historical Roman blessing; ongoing in some traditional Roman-rite parishes
attestations.evidence_note: Direct traditional-parish documentation and another Catholic parish's independent historical explanation support 27 December priestly blessing of wine, not a general medicinal or universal practice.

attestations.period_label: Historical Roman Ritual forms; regionally rooted continuing Easter practice
attestations.evidence_note: The historical Roman Ritual contains specific food blessings; diocesan and Vatican popular-piety sources identify the optional regional household custom and Easter table. No parish/place or universal scheduling claim is implied.

attestations.period_label: Catholic family Advent practice, contemporary episcopal witness
attestations.evidence_note: WEI58-05-002. USCCB documents a household Advent wreath and a family member leading home prayer; independent of Weiser's historical-origin assertions.

attestations.period_label: Traditional attribution to French custom; independently documented in a Catholic US family in 2014
attestations.evidence_note: WEI58-05-005. The 2014 account specifically documents household straw added after good deeds; no evidence for universal French prevalence.

attestations.period_label: Traditional Catholic Mexican and wider Latin American Advent practice; USCCB modern confirmation
attestations.evidence_note: WEI58-05-011. USCCB identifies 16 December and Latin American communal singing and door-to-door reenactment.

attestations.period_label: Polish Catholic heritage observed in families and a US parish
attestations.evidence_note: WEI58-06-009, WEI58-09-007. Parish documents wafers at family supper, home sharing, optional priestly blessing and distinction from Holy Communion.

attestations.period_label: Longstanding Catholic lay pilgrimage custom; 2026 diocesan press witness
attestations.evidence_note: WEI58-15-015. Contemporary diocesan article confirms voluntary tradition, explains that fewer or more than seven churches may be visited.

attestations.period_label: 1956 independently documented Catholic family handbook practice
attestations.evidence_note: WEI58-04-003. Independent 1956 Catholic family source describes Rogation prayers and family procession for crops.

attestations.period_label: Historically attested or current bounded local Catholic practice
attestations.evidence_note: WEI58-12-013. German Kindermissionswerk directly documents carol singers visiting homes between Christmas and Epiphany for charitable solidarity.

attestations.period_label: Historically attested or current bounded local Catholic practice
attestations.evidence_note: WEI58-12-017, WEI58-12-018. The French Bishops' Conference describes the galette, fève and additional portion for a poor guest.

attestations.period_label: Historically attested or current bounded local Catholic practice
attestations.evidence_note: WEI58-21-009, WEI58-21-007. UNESCO documents Polish flower carpets; Holy See Directory 162 supports flowers on streets and windows.

attestations.period_label: Historically attested or current bounded local Catholic practice
attestations.evidence_note: WEI58-16-028. Munich-Freising Archdiocese documents German/Austrian Emmaus walks connected to Luke 24.

attestations.period_label: Historically attested or current bounded local Catholic practice
attestations.evidence_note: WEI58-13-011. Catholic Culture documents practical household Mary gardens, without independently establishing legends about particular plant names.

attestations.period_label: Historically and pastorally documented but regionally variable
attestations.evidence_note: The Holy See describes Epiphany door markings in its modern Directory on Popular Piety §118. Irish episcopal guidance records family marking and prayer. Weiser (1958, printed p. 149) documents the priestly Epiphany house blessing and subsequent chalking; Weller transmits the historical priestly formulary. Both differ from optional family marking described by contemporary Catholic pastoral sources. No universal duty or local availability is inferred.

attestations.period_label: Historical Catholic households, differing practices; no universal fixed date
attestations.evidence_note: Historical 1958 custom witness and modern Catholic liturgical commentary support removing the Nativity crib on Candlemas as one optional choice. No claim is made about an entire country, the end of the 1962 Christmas season or mandated decorations.
